blocks.text: 3.2.2 Bounds, Incumbents and Pruning

Lesson 3.2.1 solved GridCap's tiny portfolio by branching until every leaf was infeasible or integral: 29 nodes for 8 projects. The same rule on the small portfolio would grow with its 40 projects, and the planners' real portfolios are larger still. Yet the tiny tree held a hint. A whole subtree below a node with LP value 3,054.7 was searched after a plan worth 2,833 was known and before the plan worth 3,627 turned up, and nothing in that subtree could ever have won.

This lesson adds the rule that skips such subtrees. It needs two numbers at every moment of the search: the best plan found so far, and the most any unexplored part of the tree could still be worth. Comparing them is the "bound" half of branch-and-bound, and it is what lets a solver prove a plan optimal without looking at most plans.
The Model
Unchanged from lesson 3.2.1: the one-period selection model on GridCap tiny.
**Sets.** $`P`$, the projects; $`M \subseteq P`$, the must-do projects; $`C \subseteq P`$, the projects with a parent $`p(c)`$; $`\mathcal{G}`$, the alternative groups.
**Parameters.** $`c_i`$, capex ($k); $`v_i`$, value ($k); $`B`$, the capital budget ($k).
**Variables.** $`x_i \in \{0, 1\}`$ for every $`i \in P`$: 1 if project $`i`$ is funded.
**Objective and constraints.**

\begin{aligned}
\max \;& \sum_{i \in P} v_i\, x_i \\
\text{s.t. }& \sum_{i \in P} c_i\, x_i \le B && \text{(budget)} \\
& x_i = 1 \quad \forall i \in M && \text{(must}_i) \\
& x_c \le x_{p(c)} \quad \forall c \in C && \text{(parent}_c) \\
& \textstyle\sum_{i \in g} x_i \le 1 \quad \forall g \in \mathcal{G} && \text{(alt}_g)
\end{aligned}
**A node.** Branching has fixed some variables: $`F_0`$ at 0 and $`F_1`$ at 1. The node's LP is the relaxation with those fixings:

z(F_0, F_1) = \max \Big\{ \sum_{i \in P} v_i x_i \;:\; \text{the rows above},\ 0 \le x_i \le 1,\
x_i = 0 \ \forall i \in F_0,\ x_i = 1 \ \forall i \in F_1 \Big\}
with $`z = -\infty`$ when that LP is infeasible. The root is $`F_0 = F_1 = \varnothing`$.
The Incumbent Is the Best Plan Found So Far, and Its Value Is a Lower Bound

The **incumbent** is the best real plan the search has found so far: a 0-1 plan that obeys every row. Write its value $`\underline{z}`$. Because it is a real plan, the best plan is worth at least that much:
z^* \;\ge\; \underline{z}

where $`z^*`$ is the optimum, the value of the best plan. So the incumbent's value is a **lower bound** on the optimum, the mirror of lesson 3.2.1's upper bound. Before the first plan is found there is no incumbent, and the lower bound is $`-\infty`$.
In the trees of this module an incumbent appears when a node's LP is integral. Lesson 3.3.3 shows the other ways solvers find plans, such as rounding an LP solution and repairing it.
A Node's LP Value Is an Upper Bound on Every Plan Below It

Lesson 3.1.2 showed that the root's LP value bounds every plan from above. The same argument works at any node: every 0-1 plan that obeys the rows and the node's fixings is a point of the node's LP, so no plan below the node is worth more than $`z(F_0, F_1)`$. And because a child only adds a fixing, a child's LP value is never above its parent's: going down the tree, the upper bounds fall.

That gives a node two numbers to compare: the most anything below it could be worth, and the incumbent's value. If the first is not above the second, nothing below the node can improve on the incumbent.
Prune a Node That Is Infeasible, Integral, or Cannot Beat the Incumbent
A node is **pruned** (the search stops below it) for exactly three reasons:

rows: the node's LP has no solution
no plan obeys the node's rows and fixings
no plan below is worth more than the incumbent
the LP solution is all 0 and 1
it is the best plan in the node; it becomes the incumbent if it beats it

blocks.text: Every other node is branched on. The bound test is the new one. In `bnb.py` it is `can_beat`:

`search.value` is $`\underline{z}`$, or `None` before the first plan. A bound equal to the incumbent is pruned too: a plan below could at best tie, and a tie is no improvement. `EPS` keeps float noise from turning a tie into a win. `round_bound` is the next rule's subject. `bound == math.inf` is the root, which has no parent bound yet.
The search applies the test in this order: infeasible first, then the bound, then integrality. So an integral node worth less than the incumbent is recorded as pruned by bound, not as a new plan.
The rest of the loop (integral and branch) is the code lesson 3.2.1 showed. Run on tiny with pruning on:

The first 13 lines are the same as in lesson 3.2.1: until node 13 there is no incumbent, so nothing can be pruned by bound. Then node 5 (P003 funded, P001 not) has LP value 2,802.2, below the 2,833 already in hand. In lesson 3.2.1 that node was split, its subtree took 9 nodes, and it found nothing better. Here it is one line, and the tree shrinks from 29 nodes to 21 with the same answer. Node numbers follow the order nodes are made, so from here on they differ from lesson 3.2.1's.

Nodes 19 and 17 are pruned by bound too, though they would have been leaves anyway. Node 17's LP solution, worth 2,782, is a real plan; lesson 3.2.1's tree (as node 25) marked it "integral: 2,782 is no better". The bound test ran first and pruned it, which is the same decision.

The last node, 15, is integral at 3,627. Nothing is left waiting, so the search stops, and the incumbent is the optimum: every other part of the tree was pruned for one of the three reasons, so no plan anywhere beats 3,627.
With Whole-Number Values, Round the Bound Down Before Comparing

GridCap's values are whole numbers of $k, and every plan's value is a sum of them, so every plan is worth a whole number. If a node's LP bound is 25,336.4, no plan below it is worth more than 25,336. Against an incumbent of 25,336, that node cannot win, even though its unrounded bound is higher:

a node with LP bound 25,336.4 against an incumbent of 25,336: prune after rounding
small, bound rounded down: False  821 nodes, 821 LPs, best 25,336
small, bound rounded down: True   803 nodes, 802 LPs, best 25,336

The second and third lines run the whole search on GridCap small, 40 projects, with the test $`\lfloor z(F_0, F_1) \rfloor \le \underline{z}`$ instead of $`z(F_0, F_1) \le \underline{z}`$. Rounding prunes nodes whose LP bound is less than $1k above the incumbent, and saves 18 nodes. In the rounded run one node is pruned before its LP is solved (803 nodes, 802 LPs): a waiting node carries its parent's LP value as its bound, and by the time it is taken a better incumbent may already have made that bound useless.

The rule needs every objective coefficient to be a whole number and every variable integer. A model with one continuous variable in the objective, or a value like 12.5, cannot use it as is (scaling by 2 would make 12.5 whole again). GridCap keeps money in whole $k, so the rule applies to every model in this module.
<!-- practice 1 -->
The Optimum Always Lies Between the Incumbent and the Best Waiting Bound

At any moment during the search, the optimum is trapped between two numbers. The incumbent's value $`\underline{z}`$ is below it, as the first rule showed. Above it: every plan not yet ruled out lies below some waiting node, and each waiting node carries an upper bound (its parent's LP value, since its own LP is not solved yet). So
\underline{z} \;\le\; z^* \;\le\; \bar z = \max\Big(\underline{z},\ \max_{\text{waiting nodes } n} \text{bound}(n)\Big)

$`\bar z`$ is the **best bound**. The incumbent is included in the maximum because, when every waiting bound is below the incumbent, the incumbent itself is the best there is. The tiny search, printed each time the range changes:

where the optimum can be, printed each time the range changes
after node  0: between no plan yet and 3,770.1
after node 13: between 2,833 and 3,770.1
after node  1: between 2,833 and 3,695.5
after node 15: between 3,627 and 3,627.0

`step.waiting_bound` is the largest bound among the nodes still waiting after the step. The upper end stays at the root's 3,770.1 until node 1 is solved, because node 1 waited all that time with the root's value as its bound. The lower end jumps twice, at each new incumbent. When the two meet, the incumbent is proven optimal, and the search can stop even if nodes are still waiting.

The distance between the two ends, $`\bar z - \underline{z}`$, is the **gap**. Lesson 3.3.4 finds both ends and the gap in HiGHS's log, and lesson 3.4.1 shows how to stop a search once the gap is small enough.
<!-- practice 2 -->
A Good Plan Found Early Prunes More

Pruning by bound needs an incumbent, and the tiny search spent its first 13 nodes without one. A plan known before the search starts can serve as the first incumbent. A cheap one: solve the root LP and round every fractional variable down. On this model that is always a real plan: lowering a variable never breaks the budget row or an alternative group, the must-do variables are fixed at 1 and never fractional, and a child at a fraction is at most its parent's fraction, so it rounds down too.

plan = [pid for pid, v in root.x.items() if v > 1 - 1e-6]          # round the root LP down
value = sum(portfolio.project(pid).value for pid in plan)
cost = sum(portfolio.project(pid).capex for pid in plan)

tiny: root LP rounded down funds 3 projects, cost 6,850 of 7,390, value 3,504
  no starting plan:       21 nodes, best 3,627
  rounded plan to beat:    9 nodes, best 3,627
small: root LP rounded down funds 20 projects, cost 37,060 of 38,390, value 24,671
  no starting plan:      821 nodes, best 25,336
  rounded plan to beat:  655 nodes, best 25,336

On tiny, an incumbent of 3,504 from the start prunes the whole subtree under $`x_{P003} = 1`$ as soon as its LP value, 3,054.7, is known, and the search takes 9 nodes instead of 21. On small it saves 166 nodes. The answer is the same both times; only the work changes. A method that finds plans without proving them best is a **primal heuristic**, and lesson 3.3.3 covers the ones MILP solvers run before and during the search.
Summary

items: **The incumbent is the best plan found so far, and its value is a lower bound** on the optimum.
**A node's LP value is an upper bound on every plan below it**, and it never rises going down.
**Prune a node that is infeasible, integral, or cannot beat the incumbent.** Test in that order; a bound equal to the incumbent is pruned.
**With whole-number values, round the bound down before comparing.** It needs integer variables and whole objective coefficients.
**The optimum always lies between the incumbent and the best waiting bound.** When they meet, the incumbent is proven optimal.
**A good plan found early prunes more.** Rounding the root LP down gave a starting plan that cut the tiny tree from 21 nodes to 9.

a node's LP value, an upper bound on every plan below it
the best bound: the largest of $`\underline{z}`$ and the waiting nodes' bounds
the node's LP has no solution
$`z(F_0, F_1) \le \underline{z}`$, or $`\lfloor z(F_0, F_1) \rfloor \le \underline{z}`$ with whole values
the LP solution is all 0 and 1; update the incumbent if it is better

blocks.text: MathOpt reports the two ends of the range on every MILP result: `result.termination.objective_bounds.primal_bound` is the incumbent's value and `dual_bound` the best bound (lesson 3.4.1 reads them).

**Further reading:** [MathOpt `ObjectiveBounds` and `SolveResult` (OR-Tools source)](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/python/result.py) (the primal bound is a plan's value, the dual bound a value no plan beats; for a MIP solver it comes from relaxations such as the LP); [Mixed-Integer Programming (OR-Tools)](https://developers.google.com/optimization/mip) (the branch-and-bound solvers OR-Tools wraps); [Integer Programming, Chapter 9 of Applied Mathematical Programming (MIT 15.053)](https://web.mit.edu/15.053/www/AMP-Chapter-09.pdf) (section 9.5 names the three prunes fathoming by infeasibility, integrality and bounds, rounds an LP bound of 41¼ down to 41 because the objective is integral, and takes the upper bound as the best "hanging" node); [HiGHS terminology: MIP](https://ergo-code.github.io/HiGHS/dev/terminology/) (primal bound, dual bound and the gap between them, as HiGHS uses the words).
Challenges

items: In the tiny trace, node 1 waited from the first step to the fifteenth with bound 3,770.1. If the search had taken node 1 right after the root, which nodes of the $`x_{P003} = 1`$ subtree would still be solved? (Lesson 3.2.3 runs this.)
Give `branch_and_bound` the start plan P001, P002, P005, P007 and P008, worth 2,782 (check that it obeys every row first). Predict whether it prunes more or less than the rounded plan, then run it.
A model maximizes $`3.5a + 2b`$ over integers. Can it round its bounds down? What single change to the objective lets it?

blocks.text: Design Note: Why the Bound Test Runs Before the Integrality Test

An integral node worth less than the incumbent could be recorded either way; both stop the search there. Testing the bound first means the incumbent is never replaced by a worse plan, without a separate comparison. More importantly, in a real solver the bound test can run *before* the node's LP is solved, using the parent's value, as happened once in the rounded run on small. A node pruned that way costs nothing. Lesson 3.2.3 shows a node order under which this happens often.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**pruning_trace.py.** The tiny tree with pruning by bound, then the range the optimum must lie in (*Prune a Node That Is Infeasible, Integral, or Cannot Beat the Incumbent* and *The Optimum Always Lies Between the Incumbent and the Best Waiting Bound*). *Try:* Run it with `prune=False`. Predict when the range's lower end first moves and whether the upper end moves sooner.

**rounded_bound.py.** The small search with and without rounding the bound down (*With Whole-Number Values, Round the Bound Down Before Comparing*). *Try:* Add 0.5 to every project's value in a copy. Predict whether rounding still saves nodes, and why it is no longer allowed.

**head_start.py.** Rounds the root LP down and uses that plan as the first incumbent, on tiny and small (*A Good Plan Found Early Prunes More*). *Try:* Start from a worse plan, P002 alone. Predict the node count on tiny.
**bnb.py.** The branch-and-bound library; `can_beat` is the bound test.
